chunks: Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Qattan narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Zakariya al-Qattan narrated to us, saying: Bakr ibn Abdullah ibn Habib narrated to us, saying: Tamim ibn Buhloul narrated to us, from his father, from Abdullah ibn al-Fadl al-Hashimi, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the meaning of the sending of peace during prayer, so he said: The sending of peace is a sign of safety and a dissolution of the prayer. I said: And how is that, may I be sacrificed for you? He said: People used to, in the past, when an arriving person would send peace upon him, they were safe from his evil, and when they would respond to him, he was safe from their evil, and if he would not send peace, they were not safe from him, and if they would not respond to the sender of peace, he was not safe from them. That is a tradition among the Arabs, and so the sending of peace was made a sign of leaving the (state of) prayer and (a declaration of) allowability to speak and a (shield of) safety from there to enter into the prayer that which invalidates it. Moreover, the Peace is a Name from the Names of Allah, Exalted and Glorious is He, and it is performed by the praying person upon the Two Angels of Allah that have been appointed with him.
ai.seo_question: What is the theological and historical significance of saying 'As-Salam' at the end of Islamic prayer?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elucidates that the final salam functions as a ritual marker of safety and the transition from the sacred state of prayer to ordinary speech, rooted in pre-Islamic Arab customs where greetings guaranteed security. He further elevates this act by linking it to the Divine Name 'As-Salam', noting that the worshipper extends peace to the recording angels, thereby integrating human ritual with cosmic reverence. This explanation highlights the theological depth of a seemingly simple gesture, connecting social etiquette with spiritual purification and divine attributes.
